notes: Ruling slot 21 = National Union, renamed People's National Action (ANP) at its congress of February 1970 (second period). Coalition slot 22 = Portuguese Army (MD sprite). 13 = Caetano's modernising technocrats; 0 = DGS political police (ex-PIDE, renamed Nov 1969); 6 = Salazarist ultras around President Tomás; 7 = CONCP (MPLA/PAIGC/FRELIMO umbrella), since the African provinces belong to POR in 1970. ASP in 3 gets the Socialist Party as a second period from its exile founding (19 Apr 1973). Islamic slots are anchored in the Muslim communities of Mozambique, Guinea and Lisbon. Monarchists follow MD (House of Braganza, sprite).

0.name: Direcção-Geral de Segurança
0.text:
The Directorate-General of Security is Portugal's political police, the name given in November 1969 to the dreaded PIDE as part of Marcelo Caetano's cosmetic reforms. Under its long-serving director, Major Fernando da Silva Pais, it keeps files on hundreds of thousands of citizens, runs informers in factories, barracks and universities, and holds political prisoners at Caxias, Peniche and the Tarrafal camp in Cape Verde.

The DGS sees itself as a bulwark of the West against communism, liaising with NATO intelligence services and with its South African and Rhodesian counterparts. In Africa it runs its own intelligence and counter-insurgency networks against the liberation movements. Its leverage lies in fear, in its files on the regime's own elite and in its indispensability to a state fighting three colonial wars.

1.name: Ala Liberal
1.text:
The Liberal Wing is the informal group of reform-minded deputies elected to the National Assembly in October 1969 on the regime's own lists, at Marcelo Caetano's invitation. Its leading figures are the Porto lawyer Francisco Sá Carneiro, the publisher Francisco Pinto Balsemão, the neurologist João Pedro Miller Guerra, José Pedro Pinto Leite and the young Azorean João Bosco Mota Amaral.

The group wants Caetano's promised 'evolution' to mean real liberalisation: an end to censorship, freedom of association, independent courts and honest elections, together with a political rather than purely military answer in Africa and closer ties to the European Communities. It is Catholic, Western and middle-class in outlook. Its leverage rests on its legitimacy inside the Assembly and on the hopes of the modern urban professions.

2.name: Grande Oriente Lusitano
2.text:
The Lusitanian Grand Orient is Portugal's principal Masonic obedience and the old engine room of the liberal and republican tradition that made the revolution of 1910. Outlawed by Salazar's law against secret societies in 1935, it lost its Lisbon headquarters to the Portuguese Legion and survives in clandestinity, its lodges meeting discreetly in private homes.

The Grand Orient stands for the heritage of the First Republic: parliamentary government, secular schooling, separation of Church and State and civil liberties. Its members are lawyers, doctors, officers and teachers, many of them veterans of the republican opposition and of the 1949 presidential campaign of its former Grand Master, General Norton de Matos. Firmly Western in outlook, it works through personal networks rather than mass organisation.

3.name: Acção Socialista Portuguesa
3.text:
Portuguese Socialist Action was founded in Geneva in 1964 by Mário Soares, Francisco Ramos da Costa and Manuel Tito de Morais as a small clandestine group bridging exiles and activists at home. Soares, a Lisbon lawyer deported to São Tomé in 1968 and allowed back by Caetano, led the opposition's CEUD lists in the October 1969 elections, which won no seats amid fraud and harassment.

ASP is democratic socialist and resolutely Western, refusing communist tutelage and seeking recognition from the Socialist International and European social democracy. It calls for free elections, the restoration of civil liberties and self-determination for the colonies. Its base is small and intellectual – lawyers, journalists and professionals in Lisbon and Porto – but its foreign contacts give it outsized standing.

3.name: Partido Socialista
3.text:
The Socialist Party was founded on 19 April 1973 at Bad Münstereifel in West Germany, when the congress of Portuguese Socialist Action, hosted by the Friedrich Ebert Foundation, voted to transform itself into a party. Mário Soares, living in exile in Paris, was elected secretary-general.

The party is democratic socialist, Western and pro-European, firmly allied with the Socialist International and determined to stand apart from the communists while cooperating with them against the dictatorship. It demands democracy, an end to the colonial wars and negotiated independence for the colonies. Its organisation inside Portugal remains thin, but its international backing makes it the obvious democratic alternative.

4.name: Partido Comunista Português
4.text:
The Portuguese Communist Party, founded in 1921, has been illegal since 1926 and is the best-organised force of the opposition. Its secretary-general Álvaro Cunhal, who escaped from the Peniche fortress in January 1960, directs the party from exile in Moscow and Paris, while an underground apparatus of full-time functionaries prints the newspaper Avante! and runs cells inside Portugal under constant police pursuit.

The PCP is orthodox and loyal to Moscow, having endorsed the invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968. It calls for a 'democratic and national revolution' against fascism and the monopolies, an end to the colonial wars and independence for the colonies. Its strongholds are the landless labourers of the Alentejo, the industrial belt around Lisbon, the students and much of the intelligentsia.

5.name: Liga de Unidade e Acção Revolucionária
5.english: League of Revolutionary Unity and Action
5.native_full: Liga de Unidade e Acção Revolucionária
5.text:
The League of Revolutionary Unity and Action was founded in 1967 by Hermínio da Palma Inácio, a legendary adventurer of the anti-Salazar resistance, after a spectacular raid on the Bank of Portugal branch at Figueira da Foz financed its first operations. Palma Inácio was captured in 1968 while preparing to seize the town of Covilhã, but escaped from prison in Porto and is again active from exile, with comrades such as Camilo Mortágua.

LUAR rejects both the PCP's caution and the moderates' legalism, arguing that only armed action can topple the dictatorship and end the colonial wars. Its politics are a loose revolutionary socialism with libertarian accents. Small and conspiratorial, it draws on exiles in Paris and young militants at home, and its leverage lies in daring rather than numbers.

6.name: Os Ultras
6.text:
The Ultras are the regime's die-hard Salazarists, who see Marcelo Caetano's 'renewal in continuity' as the first step towards surrender. They look to President Américo Tomás, who holds the power to dismiss the prime minister, and count among their own the former foreign minister Alberto Franco Nogueira, now a deputy, General Kaúlza de Arriaga and much of the old guard of the National Union and the Portuguese Legion.

They hold that Portugal is a single nation from Minho to Timor and that the overseas provinces are not negotiable. Embittered by American and United Nations hostility to the colonial wars, they distrust Washington and the liberal West, preferring Salazar's 'proudly alone' and the friendship of Pretoria and Salisbury. Their leverage lies in Belém palace, the officer corps and the censorship.

7.name: Conferência das Organizações Nacionalistas das Colónias Portuguesas
7.english: Conference of Nationalist Organizations of the Portuguese Colonies
7.native_full: Conferência das Organizações Nacionalistas das Colónias Portuguesas
7.text:
The Conference of Nationalist Organizations of the Portuguese Colonies was founded in Casablanca in April 1961 to coordinate the movements fighting Portuguese rule. It links the MPLA of Agostinho Neto in Angola, the PAIGC of Amílcar Cabral in Guinea and Cape Verde, and FRELIMO in Mozambique, led since the assassination of Eduardo Mondlane in February 1969 by a council including Samora Machel and Marcelino dos Santos, the CONCP's secretary-general.

The CONCP movements wage guerrilla war in all three African theatres and seek complete independence, social revolution and the political mobilisation of the peasantry under a single vanguard. Armed by the Soviet Union, the Eastern bloc, Cuba and China, and hosted by Algeria, Tanzania, Zambia and Guinea, they are the regime's mortal enemy and the decisive check on its imperial future.
7.wiki: Conference of Nationalist Organizations of the Portuguese Colonies

8.name: Comunidade Ismaili de Moçambique
8.text:
The Ismaili Community of Mozambique gathers the followers of the Aga Khan, mostly families of Gujarati origin, in Lourenço Marques, Beira, Nampula and the trading towns of the interior. Organised around its jamatkhanas and councils under Prince Karim Aga Khan IV, Imam since 1957, it is one of the most prosperous and best-organised minorities in the overseas provinces.

The community practises a modernist Shia Islam that prizes education, health care, the advancement of women and loyalty to the state of residence. It keeps carefully apart from politics and has cultivated correct relations with the Portuguese authorities, who value its commerce. Its leverage lies in wealth, in networks across East Africa and the Indian Ocean, and in the Aga Khan's international prestige.

9.name: Círculo de Najaf
9.text:
The Najaf Circle is a small group of Twelver Shia merchants and young men of Indian origin in Lourenço Marques and Beira, linked to the Khoja Ithna-Asheri communities of East Africa and to the great seminaries of Iraq. They follow Grand Ayatollah Muhsin al-Hakim as their marja' and pass around the sermons of the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who teaches in Najaf.

The circle believes that Muslims should be guided by the senior clergy in public as well as private life, and it is hostile to Western secularism and communism alike. Under Portuguese rule it keeps strictly to religious and charitable work, collecting religious dues for Najaf. Its influence is confined to a few families, but its ties abroad give it a voice beyond its numbers.

10.name: Comunidade Islâmica de Lisboa
10.text:
The Islamic Community of Lisbon was founded in March 1968 by Muslim university students and professionals from Mozambique, with Suleiman Valy Mamede as a leading figure, to give the few Muslims of metropolitan Portugal a legal association and, in time, a mosque in the capital. It enjoys the benevolence of a regime eager to show the Muslim world that Portugal respects Islam.

The community preaches loyalty to the state and to a multiracial, multi-faith Portugal, in step with the government's Islamic policy, which courts the sheikhs of the Sufi brotherhoods of northern Mozambique and the Fula chiefs of Guinea against the liberation movements. Its leverage is modest in Lisbon but real overseas, where more than a million Muslims are a prize in the war for hearts and minds.

11.name: Hizb ut-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation, was founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by the Islamic judge Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, who leads it from exile in Beirut. Banned throughout the Arab world, it organises in secret cells in Jordan, Iraq, Syria and Lebanon and among Arab students in Western Europe; in the Portuguese world it reaches only a few foreign students in Lisbon and Coimbra.

The party rejects nationalism, democracy and communism alike as un-Islamic and works to restore the Caliphate, preferably by winning over army officers for a coup. Its members study al-Nabhani's books and draft constitution in disciplined circles. Without a real base in Portugal or its colonies, its leverage lies in an ideology that answers both colonialism and the secular liberation movements.

12.name: Os Azharistas
12.text:
The Azharites are a loose network of Mozambican and Guinean Muslims who studied at al-Azhar in Cairo, in Sudan or in the Hijaz and have come home with reformist ideas. Teachers and preachers in the mosques and Koranic schools of Lourenço Marques, Ilha de Moçambique and Bissau, they are watched closely by the DGS, which suspects Nasser's Egypt of using Islamic scholarships to recruit for the liberation movements.

They want Muslims to return to scripture, abandon the rites of the Sufi brotherhoods and build modern Islamic schools teaching Arabic alongside secular subjects. They are wary both of the Portuguese state and of the secular nationalism of FRELIMO and the PAIGC. Their leverage lies in education and in contacts with Egyptian, Sudanese and Saudi patrons.

13.name: Os Tecnocratas
13.text:
The Technocrats are the young economists, engineers and managers Marcelo Caetano brought into government after succeeding Salazar in 1968, to modernise Portugal without dismantling the regime. Their figureheads are Rogério Martins, Secretary of State for Industry, and João Salgueiro, Under-Secretary of State for Planning, backed by the planners of the Third Development Plan of 1968–1973.

They believe growth, industrialisation and closer ties with Europe will defuse political tension better than repression, and they push to dismantle industrial licensing, attract foreign capital and extend social security to rural workers. Politically cautious and loyal to Caetano, they care little for ideology. Their leverage lies in the economic ministries, in business demand for their reforms and in the prime minister's own sympathy.

14.name: Igreja Católica em Portugal
14.text:
The Catholic Church in Portugal, led by Cardinal Manuel Gonçalves Cerejeira, Patriarch of Lisbon since 1929 and Salazar's friend since their student days at Coimbra, has been a pillar of the Estado Novo and is bound to it by the Concordat of 1940. Its hierarchy blesses the regime's 'God, Fatherland, Family', and Fátima has become the spiritual centre of the nation.

Yet the Church is no longer of one mind. Since the Second Vatican Council a progressive minority of priests and lay Catholics has protested against the colonial wars and censorship, and the Bishop of Porto, António Ferreira Gomes, exiled in 1959 for criticising Salazar, returned to his diocese in 1969. The hierarchy remains conservative and anti-communist, its power resting on parishes, schools and the deep piety of the north.

15.name: Companhia União Fabril
15.text:
The Companhia União Fabril is the largest industrial group in the Iberian Peninsula, built by Alfredo da Silva and now run by his grandsons Jorge and José Manuel de Mello. From its chemical works at Barreiro it has expanded into shipbuilding and ship repair, tobacco, textiles, insurance, banking, shipping and colonial plantations, employing tens of thousands of workers.

CUF heads the handful of family groups – Mello, Espírito Santo, Champalimaud and a few others – that dominate the Portuguese economy under the protection of the corporative state and industrial licensing. They want stability, cheap labour, guaranteed colonial markets and a gradual opening to Europe on their own terms. Their leverage lies in interlocking boards, access to ministers and their indispensability to the war economy.

16.name: Associação Comercial de Lisboa
16.text:
The Lisbon Commercial Association, founded in 1834, is the oldest business body in Portugal and the voice of the capital's merchants, importers, exporters and colonial trading houses. Integrated into the corporative system yet jealous of its independence, it speaks for commerce against an industrial policy that has long favoured protected monopolies.

The association argues for free trade within EFTA, which Portugal joined as a founding member in 1960, and for an open market between the metropole and the overseas provinces. It opposes industrial licensing, price controls and red tape, and looks to the European Communities as Portugal's natural future. Its leverage rests on its members' place in foreign trade and its standing with the economic ministries.

17.name: Liga para a Protecção da Natureza
17.english: League for the Protection of Nature
17.native_full: Liga para a Protecção da Natureza
17.text:
The League for the Protection of Nature, founded in 1948, is the oldest environmental association in the Iberian Peninsula. It was born of the campaign to save the ancient forest of the Serra da Arrábida, championed by the poet Sebastião da Gama, and brings together naturalists, foresters, university scientists and educated amateurs, mostly in Lisbon.

The League campaigns for nature reserves, the protection of wildlife and landscapes, and against the uncontrolled building spreading along the coast with the tourist boom. It is apolitical and conservative in temper, careful not to provoke the censors. Its leverage is small but growing as industrialisation, eucalyptus plantations and dams transform the countryside, and it presses for the country's first national park.

18.name: Comissão Democrática Eleitoral
18.text:
The Democratic Electoral Commission emerged for the October 1969 elections as the broad front of the democratic opposition, uniting communists and their sympathisers, progressive Catholics, old republicans and independent socialists. Led in Lisbon by the Catholic economist Francisco Pereira de Moura, it won no seats under the regime's rigged rules but drew large crowds, and its committees have stayed active.

The CDE calls for civil liberties, an amnesty for political prisoners, free trade unions, an end to the colonial wars and negotiations with the liberation movements. Neutralist in temper rather than pro-Soviet, it insists on the unity of all anti-fascists. Its base lies among students, white-collar workers, the urban professions and the progressive Catholic milieu, and its leverage is mobilisation whenever the regime permits a campaign.

19.name: Comité Marxista-Leninista Português
19.text:
The Portuguese Marxist-Leninist Committee was founded in 1964 by Francisco Martins Rodrigues and other dissidents who broke with the PCP, accusing Álvaro Cunhal of revisionism and of shrinking from armed struggle. Its armed wing, the Popular Action Front, was crushed by the political police; Martins Rodrigues has been in prison since 1966, and the movement has splintered into rival groups of students and young workers.

The committee follows Mao Zedong's line, condemning Soviet 'social-imperialism' as fiercely as fascism and colonialism, and calls for a people's revolutionary war, alliance with the African liberation movements and the dictatorship of the proletariat. Its militants are few, young and mostly students in Lisbon, Coimbra and the Paris exile, but they are the most radical voice against the colonial war.

20.name: Legião Portuguesa
20.text:
The Portuguese Legion is the regime's paramilitary militia, founded in 1936 in the heat of the Spanish Civil War to defend the Estado Novo against communism. Its legionaries, organised in brigades and commanded by army officers, wear the green shirt, man civil defence and act as the eyes and ears of the political police in workplaces and neighbourhoods.

The Legion is militantly nationalist, anti-communist and imperial, contemptuous of liberals and suspicious of Caetano's opening. It cultivates the cult of the soldiers in Africa and of a Portugal that is 'one and indivisible'. Its ageing ranks give it less muscle than in the 1930s, but it remains a reservoir of street-level loyalism and informers for the hard right of the regime.

21.name: União Nacional
21.text:
The National Union is the single political organisation of the Estado Novo, founded by António de Oliveira Salazar in 1930 as a civic association rather than a party, to rally support for the dictatorship. Since Salazar's incapacitation in September 1968 it is led by the new prime minister, Marcelo Caetano, whose lists took every seat in the National Assembly in the controlled elections of October 1969.

The movement defends the corporative state, the Catholic social order, 'God, Fatherland and Family' and the integrity of a multicontinental nation from Minho to Timor. Caetano wants to rename and revitalise it as a vehicle for his cautious 'evolution', opening it to younger technocrats and liberals. Its leverage lies in its monopoly of candidacies, the civil service and the local notables of the countryside.

21.name: Acção Nacional Popular
21.text:
People's National Action is the new name Marcelo Caetano gives the regime's single political organisation, the National Union, at its congress in February 1970. The change is meant to signal his 'renewal in continuity', bringing younger cadres, technocrats and liberal deputies into a movement run for four decades by Salazar's notables.

The ANP keeps the essentials of the Estado Novo: the corporative state, the Catholic social order, the ban on parties and the defence of the overseas provinces as an indivisible part of Portugal. Under Caetano it promises social progress, development and a measure of political modernisation, while hardliners within it resist every concession. Its strength lies in its monopoly of candidacies, the state apparatus and local patronage networks.

22.name: Exército Português
22.text:
The Portuguese Army carries the burden of three colonial wars, in Angola since 1961, in Guinea since 1963 and in Mozambique since 1964, with well over 100,000 men under arms in Africa and conscripts serving up to four years. Its leading figures include General António de Spínola, governor and commander-in-chief in Guinea, and General Kaúlza de Arriaga, commanding the land forces in Mozambique.

The officer corps is the ultimate arbiter of the regime, loyal since the coup of 1926, but it is not of one mind: hardliners demand total victory, while men like Spínola doubt there is a purely military solution. Conscript officers from the universities and overstretched career captains carry the weight of the war. Its leverage is decisive: no Portuguese government survives without the army.

23.name: Casa de Bragança
23.text:
The House of Braganza ruled Portugal from 1640 until the revolution of 1910. Its head is Dom Duarte Nuno, Duke of Braganza, heir of the Miguelist line, who settled in Portugal in 1952 after the law of banishment was repealed; his son Dom Duarte Pio is serving as an air force officer in Angola. The Monarchist Cause keeps the royalist flame alive among aristocrats, landowners and Catholic intellectuals.

The monarchists favour a traditional, Catholic and corporative monarchy as the natural crown of Portuguese history and the guarantee of national unity across the empire. Many have served Salazar faithfully, while some younger monarchists have joined the democratic opposition. Their leverage is limited, resting on prestige, family networks and the Republic's lack of a popular soul.
